title: Find K-th Smallest Pair Distance
description: Brute force to optimized: generating and sorting every pair distance versus binary searching the answer distance, verified with an O(n) two-pointer count.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth smallest distance among all pairs, where the distance of a pair is the absolute difference between its two values.

blocks.text: Considering every possible pair of elements (by index) in nums, and the absolute difference of their values as that pair's "distance," find the kth smallest such distance among all pairs.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the kth Closest Pair of House Numbers on a Street
blocks.text: Picture a street of houses with various numbers, and considering the "closeness" of every pair of houses as the difference in their numbers. Finding the kth smallest such difference, among every possible pair, is the task, without needing to compute and sort every single pair's difference directly.

blocks.caption: Sort first; the count of pairs within a distance d only grows as d grows, enabling binary search

blocks.text: The pairs and their distances are (1,3)=2, (1,1)=0, (3,1)=2; sorted, the distances are 0,2,2; the 1st smallest is 0.
Every pair has distance 0 (all values equal); the 2nd smallest is still 0.

Before generating and sorting every pair's distance directly, notice that "how many pairs have distance at most d" is a value that only grows as d grows, exactly the monotonic structure binary search needs.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Sorting nums first makes it possible to count, for any candidate distance d, how many pairs have distance at most d, using a sliding two-pointer sweep in O(n).

Observation 2: As d increases, the count of qualifying pairs can only increase or stay the same, never decrease, exactly the monotonic property binary search exploits.

Observation 3: Binary searching over candidate distances d, from 0 up to the maximum possible difference, finds the smallest d whose count of qualifying pairs is at least k.

Observation 4: That smallest such d is exactly the kth smallest pair distance, since it is the boundary where the count of pairs "catches up" to k.

This leads to sorting nums, then binary searching for the smallest distance d such that the number of pairs with distance at most d is at least k, counted efficiently with a two-pointer sweep for each candidate d.
Generate every pair's distance directly, sort them all, and pick the kth smallest.

items: For every pair of indices i less than j, compute the absolute difference of nums[i] and nums[j].
Collect all these distances into a list and sort it.
Return the value at position k minus 1.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every one of the roughly n squared over 2 pairs is generated and its distance stored directly.
With n up to 10000, this produces up to 50 million distances, both slow to generate and to sort.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared log n), generating O(n squared) distances and sorting them.
Space: O(n squared) to store every distance.
Limitation: with n up to 10000, this is both too slow and too memory-heavy; a way to count qualifying pairs WITHOUT generating them all is needed.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why generating every pair is unnecessary: only the COUNT of pairs within a given distance is ever needed, not the pairs themselves, and that count can be computed directly with a sliding window on the sorted array.

How to count pairs within a distance d quickly: after sorting, for each right endpoint, slide a left pointer forward while the pair's distance exceeds d; the number of valid left positions for that right endpoint counts directly toward the total.

How binary search uses this: search over candidate distances d, using the O(n) count function to check whether at least k pairs fall within d, narrowing toward the smallest such d.

The core idea: sort nums, then binary search the answer distance, counting qualifying pairs with an O(n) two-pointer sweep at each candidate distance.

Sort nums. Binary search over candidate distances d, from 0 to the maximum possible difference. For each candidate d, count how many pairs have distance at most d using a two-pointer sweep (for each right index, advance a left index forward while the difference exceeds d, and add right minus left to the count). Narrow the binary search to the smallest d whose count is at least k.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: binary search the distance, two-pointer count for each candidate

blocks.text: After sorting, the two-pointer sweep correctly counts, for each right endpoint, exactly how many earlier elements form a pair with distance at most d, since the left pointer only ever moves forward as the window's required distance is exceeded. Since this count only grows as d grows, binary search correctly converges on the smallest d for which at least k pairs qualify, which is exactly the kth smallest pair distance.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n plus n log(max distance)), sorting once, then a binary search where each check costs O(n).
Space: O(1) extra beyond the sorted array.

blocks.text: This problem is a classic "binary search on the answer" pattern: instead of generating every pair, binary search directly over candidate distances, using an efficient counting function (a two-pointer sweep on the sorted array) to check feasibility at each candidate.

items: Forgetting to sort nums before applying the two-pointer counting technique.
Off-by-one errors in the two-pointer count, remember every position from left to right minus 1 (inclusive) forms a valid pair with the current right endpoint.

blocks.text: Framing this explicitly as "binary search on the answer, verified by a counting function" is the key insight, since it is a broadly reusable pattern beyond just this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "n is too large to generate every pair", think: binary search the answer distance, and count qualifying pairs with a two-pointer sweep instead of generating them.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared log n) time and O(n squared) space. The optimized binary-search-plus-two-pointer approach runs in O(n log(max distance)) time and O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: binary search on the answer (a candidate distance), verified by an O(n) two-pointer counting function.
Core Idea: sort nums, then binary search the smallest distance d for which at least k pairs have distance at most d, counted efficiently with a two-pointer sweep.
Time: O(n squared log n) for the brute force, O(n log(max distance)) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(1) extra for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: the count of pairs within a distance d is monotonic in d, enabling binary search instead of generating every pair.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known "binary search the answer" problem, quick once the counting function is recognized.
One line memory trick: binary search the distance, count qualifying pairs with a two-pointer sweep.
